summary:
Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and additionally carries its own state-level Sharia criminal layer. Human Rights Watch (2004) lists Niger among the twelve northern states that adopted Sharia criminal provisions, a wave traced from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law of 27 October 1999; these provisions remain in force.

Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, signed 22 February 2000, in operation 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000, amends the 1960 Penal Code so that certain offences applied to Muslims carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims. It defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68. A Muslim visitor outed in Niger State therefore stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) sets out the hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women, and notes the limits of available arrest data.

Separately, Niger's own national law has hardened sharply. Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted March 2025, criminalises all LGBTQIA+ acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts with 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs, expressly covering changing or attempting to change one's birth sex, and punishing creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues with 10 to 20 years and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties.

Since March 2025, Article 24 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman; since June 2026, marrying a person of the same sex or officiating, organising or witnessing such a wedding carries 10 to 20 years. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. After the 2026 code took effect, dozens were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding.

Enforcement incidents include two young women in Maradi prosecuted in 2022 for lesbianism, acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act; and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025, prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. Two men caught naked in a parked car were arrested for public indecency and fined.

As of December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, when Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise them, with no scheduled debate.
tangentialFactors:
Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working after the 2026 code took effect, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; Law 2015-36, which had prohibited discrimination including on sexual orientation, was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged.

Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition, faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. Gay men and lesbians face strong pressure to conform, leading many to live socially acceptable public lives while seeking relationships privately. No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness discrimination cases were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented reporting. Two gay rights organisations operate in secret, partly because they are not formally registered.

The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread public debate. The only official cultural-values statement concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values". Male prostitution was prevalent in Niamey, and effeminate men were known for organising traditional wedding ceremonies as a livelihood. Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalised in 2026; before that, the age of consent was 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts.
localsOnly:
Niger State residents who are Muslim fall under the state Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000's parallel track: section 68A subjects them to the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, including amputation, where the offence is proved to the Islamic evidentiary standard, while non-Muslims face the ordinary Penal Code penalty. This is a resident-facing distinction that does not apply identically to all defendants.

Niger's national Refoundation Charter and February 2026 penal code bind residents directly: changing or attempting to change one's birth sex is a punishable practice, and participation in LGBTQIA+ organisations carries 10 to 20 years with no mitigating circumstances or suspended sentences available. Since the 2026 code took effect, LGBTQ residents have gone into hiding and HIV prevention services for MSM have ceased operating.

Two gay rights organisations continue to work in secret, partly because they are not formally registered. Gay men and lesbians report strong societal pressure to conform, with many maintaining publicly conventional lives while pursuing relationships privately. No broad statutory protection against discrimination on gender identity or sexual orientation exists for residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
The available arrest data is limited, as the UK Home Office note itself records; the true scale of enforcement in Niger State is unresolved. Whether the February 2026 national penal code's provisions have been applied in Niger State specifically, and how many arrests have occurred there since it took effect, is not sourced here.

The interaction between Niger State's section 68A parallel track and the February 2026 national code for a Muslim defendant is not addressed in the inventory and remains unresolved. No trans-specific violence incident in Niger State is documented in these sources; the absence of reported violence nationally may reflect underreporting due to stigma or intimidation rather than its absence.
